promptText: According to the 'categories of state' framework, why shouldn't fetched API data typically be stored in a general client-state store like plain Redux or Zustand?
options: Server data is a cache of remote truth that goes stale and needs deduplication and revalidation — concerns a plain store doesn't handle, unlike a dedicated query-caching library
Redux and Zustand are technically incapable of storing objects returned from an API
Server data must always be stored in the URL instead
It is fine to store it there; there is no meaningful difference between server and client state
explanation: Server state is asynchronous, shared, and can go stale, requiring caching, deduplication, and revalidation that a plain client store has no built-in concept of — exactly the gap TanStack Query/SWR fill.

promptText: Why is React Context described as 'not really a state manager'?
options: It's a transport mechanism for passing a value down the tree; it has no built-in selector, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provided value changes, regardless of which part it reads
Context can only hold string values, not objects or functions
Context requires Redux to be installed as a peer dependency
Context cannot be combined with useReducer
explanation: Context carries a value down the tree but has no subscription granularity; the state itself still needs to live in useState/useReducer, and every consumer re-renders on any change to the value.

promptText: A Context provider passes value={{ user, setUser }} inline on every render. What's the resulting bug and the fix?
options: A new object is created on every render, so every consumer re-renders even when user hasn't changed; the fix is to wrap the value in useMemo keyed on user
This causes a compile-time TypeScript error and will not run
It silently drops setUser from context, leaving only user accessible
It causes an infinite loop because objects cannot be passed as context values
explanation: An inline object literal has a new reference every render, so React treats the context value as changed on every parent render, re-rendering all consumers unless the value is memoized.

promptText: Splitting a reducer-backed Context into a separate StateContext and DispatchContext avoids what specific re-render problem?
options: Components that only call dispatch and never read state can subscribe to the dispatch-only context and never re-render on state changes, because dispatch from useReducer has a stable identity
It reduces the total bundle size of the reducer function
It allows state updates to skip validation entirely
It prevents the reducer from ever being called more than once
explanation: Because dispatch's identity is guaranteed stable by React, a component subscribed only to the dispatch context never re-renders when state changes, unlike one bundled context holding both.

promptText: In classic Redux, why must reducers be pure functions with no side effects?
options: Redux detects state changes by reference equality and relies on determinism for DevTools, time-travel, and SSR hydration; mutating state or performing I/O in a reducer breaks all of that
JavaScript does not allow side effects inside any function called 'reducer'
Impure reducers cause Redux to crash immediately on the first dispatch
Purity is only a style convention with no functional impact
explanation: Purity is what makes Redux's change detection, time-travel debugging, and predictable testing possible; a reducer that mutates or performs I/O silently breaks those guarantees.

promptText: In Redux Toolkit's createSlice, writing state.value += 1 inside a reducer works safely because of what mechanism?
options: createSlice wraps each case reducer in Immer's produce, which records the 'mutation' against a draft and returns a correctly-copied new immutable object
Redux Toolkit disables the immutability rule of Redux entirely by default
The += operator is specially overloaded by React to be immutable
It only works because value is a number; object fields cannot be updated this way
explanation: Immer's Proxy-based draft tracks writes and produces a structurally-shared immutable result, letting you write mutating-looking code safely inside RTK reducers.

promptText: A reselect selector createSelector([selectItems], items => items.filter(...)) is called by many different rows with different id arguments through one shared module-level selector instance. What performance problem results, and why?
options: Cache thrashing — reselect's default memoization cache holds only the most recent call's inputs and result, so alternating arguments across rows causes a cache miss and full recompute on almost every call
The selector throws a runtime TypeError when called with different arguments
Nothing — reselect automatically creates a separate cache per unique argument out of the box
It causes a memory leak that grows unbounded over time
explanation: Reselect's default cache size is one; sharing a single selector instance across many differently-parameterized callers overwrites that one cache slot constantly, defeating memoization entirely.

promptText: What problem does createAsyncThunk's rejected action exist to solve, and what breaks if a slice's extraReducers doesn't handle it?
options: It represents a failed async attempt; if unhandled, the slice stays stuck in a loading state forever after a failure, showing a spinner that never resolves and silently swallowing the error
Nothing breaks — rejected is purely optional telemetry with no state implications
The entire Redux store crashes if rejected isn't handled
It automatically retries the thunk up to three times if unhandled
explanation: If only pending and fulfilled are handled, a genuine failure (network error, 401, validation error) leaves the state's status stuck at 'loading' with no error surfaced to the UI.

promptText: What is the main practical difference between RTK Query and TanStack Query?
options: RTK Query's cache lives inside the Redux store and requires Redux; TanStack Query is framework and store agnostic and needs no global store at all
TanStack Query cannot perform mutations, only reads
RTK Query is written in a different language and cannot run in the browser
There is no meaningful difference; they are the same library under different names
explanation: Both solve server-state caching declaratively, but RTK Query integrates with an existing Redux store while TanStack Query manages its own independent cache with no store required.

promptText: Why does Zustand achieve selective re-renders without a Provider wrapping the app, unlike a Context-based store?
options: The store is a plain module-level object with subscribe and getState, and components pass a selector function to the store's hook, subscribing only to the specific slice they select
Zustand secretly uses React Context internally in exactly the same way, just hidden from the developer
Zustand stores can only hold a single primitive value, which removes the need for selectors
Zustand disables React's re-render mechanism entirely
explanation: Zustand's store lives outside React entirely; components subscribe via a selector, and only re-render when the selected slice's value actually changes, with no provider tree required.

promptText: Selecting an object literal from a Zustand store, e.g. useStore(s => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b })), re-renders the component on every store update. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Zustand compares the selector's return value with Object.is (reference equality) by default, and a fresh object literal is always 'different'; use useShallow to shallow-compare the returned fields instead
Because Zustand does not support selecting more than one field at a time under any circumstances
Because object literals are not valid return types for Zustand selectors and this throws at runtime
Because Zustand recomputes the entire store on every render regardless of the selector
explanation: The default comparison is reference equality; wrapping the selector in useShallow performs a one-level-deep comparison instead, avoiding needless re-renders from a freshly-constructed object.

promptText: In Jotai's atomic model, what does atomFamily solve that a single Redux array combined with per-row selectors does not solve as cleanly?
options: It gives each item in a dynamic collection its own independently-subscribable atom by default, so updating one row never re-renders components watching other rows without hand-written memoized per-row selectors
atomFamily makes all atoms in the app share exactly one piece of global state
atomFamily is only usable for numeric values, not objects
atomFamily removes the need to ever call useAtom in a component
explanation: Per-row isolation is atomFamily's default behavior, whereas achieving the equivalent in a single Redux array requires deliberate selector-level optimization or normalization.

promptText: Why is normalizing state (storing entities once, by id) generally preferred over embedding full copies of related entities in multiple places?
options: Denormalized or duplicated copies of the same entity can drift out of sync — updating one embedded copy doesn't update the others, causing stale-data bugs
Normalization is required by the JavaScript specification for all state objects
Denormalized data cannot be serialized to JSON at all
Normalization makes every read operation faster than a denormalized shape in all cases
explanation: When the same entity appears in multiple lists as separate copies, updating one copy leaves the others stale; storing it once by id eliminates that class of bug entirely.

promptText: What is 'structural sharing', and why is it the property that makes oldState.branch === newState.branch a valid, cheap way to detect 'no change' after an immutable update?
options: An immutable update via spreads or Immer only creates new objects along the path from the root to the changed value; every untouched branch keeps its original reference, so reference equality reliably reflects real (in)equality without a deep comparison
It means every update deep-clones the entire state tree so nothing is ever accidentally shared
It refers to sharing the same reducer function across multiple slices
It only applies when using TypeScript's structural typing system, not at runtime
explanation: Structural sharing is what makes reference-equality checks in reselect, React.memo, and useSelector both cheap and correct — unrelated branches genuinely keep their original references.

promptText: According to the state-management decision framework, when should you actually introduce a global client store such as Zustand or Redux rather than local or lifted state or the URL?
options: Only after confirming the state isn't server data, isn't URL-shaped, and isn't needed by just one component or a few nearby ones — i.e. it's genuinely cross-cutting client state needed by many unrelated parts of the tree
Immediately, any time two sibling components need to share any value
Only when the app has more than 1000 lines of code, regardless of what the state represents
Global stores should be introduced before writing any components, as a starting scaffold
explanation: The decision ladder moves from local state, to lifting/composition, to the URL, to server-cache libraries, and reaches for a global store only as a last resort for genuinely cross-cutting client state.
